name: Rhino 3D
tagline: NURBS surface and solid modeler used for industrial design, architecture, jewelry and marine work, with the Grasshopper visual scripting environment bundled in.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Rhino sells perpetual licenses rather than subscriptions, so there is no meaningful monthly figure.

verdictSummary: Rhino is a geometry kernel with a UI bolted on, and the kernel is the product. Free-form NURBS surfacing, trimming, filleting, booleans on trimmed surfaces and tolerant intersection math represent roughly thirty years of numerical engineering that nobody one-shots, or weekend-shots, or year-shots. On top of that sits Grasshopper and a plugin ecosystem that a lot of professional workflows are physically built around. An agent can absolutely give you a local script-driven CAD tool with real B-rep solids by standing on an existing open kernel, which is useful and genuinely fun. It is not Rhino, and the gap is not UI polish, it is the part underneath.
coreLoopDIY: A local Python-scripted parametric CAD workbench that builds real B-rep solids via an existing open kernel, previews them in a browser viewer, and exports STEP and STL.
requirements: Python 3.11 and a working CadQuery / OpenCascade install, which is the fiddliest part
Comfort writing geometry as code instead of dragging control points
A browser for the preview viewer
Patience with kernel error messages that read like Fortran
whatYouLose: Interactive NURBS surfacing: control point editing, sweeps, lofts, blends by hand
Tolerant modeling, the thing that lets Rhino keep going when your surfaces do not quite meet
Grasshopper, and the decade of community definitions written for it
The plugin ecosystem: rendering, nesting, jewelry, analysis, marine hull tools
File interop that other studios actually trust when you send them a 3dm or STEP
moatNotes: Odd case where execution-polish means numerical robustness rather than pretty pixels. The surface intersection code is the moat.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a perpetual license at under four figures, no subscription, with a kernel that survives messy real-world geometry and a visual scripting layer that an entire generation of architecture students learned on, is one of the better deals in professional software. People do not pay Rhino for features they could reimplement, they pay because when a client sends a scanned mesh and a half-broken IGES file at 6pm, Rhino opens both and does not explode. That reliability is not a feature list, it is accumulated bug fixes.
notes: A viewer is a weekend; a geometry kernel is not. The moat is thirty years of NURBS intersection and tolerance math, plus every Grasshopper definition written against it.
prompt:
Build a local script-driven parametric CAD workbench. This is a consolation build, not a Rhino clone: it does solid modeling as code, not interactive NURBS surfacing.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11
- CadQuery (which wraps the OpenCascade B-rep kernel) for all geometry
- FastAPI for a tiny local server
- Plain HTML plus three.js loaded from a local vendored file for the viewer
- No database, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud

What to build:
1. A models/ folder where each .py file defines a function build(params: dict) that returns a CadQuery Workplane result.
2. Each model file declares a PARAMS dict of named numeric parameters with defaults, min and max.
3. A FastAPI app that lists models, renders a parameter form from PARAMS, and on submit calls build(), tessellates the result to a mesh, and serves it as glTF or a simple JSON mesh.
4. A single-page viewer: orbit, pan, zoom, wireframe toggle, and sliders for the declared params that re-request geometry on change with debouncing.
5. Export buttons that write STEP and STL to an exports/ folder via CadQuery's exporters.
6. A file watcher that reloads a model module when its .py changes, so editing the script updates the viewer.
7. Ship three example models: a parametric enclosure with filleted edges and a lid, a flanged pipe elbow, and a gear-ish plate with a bolt circle.

Explicitly out of scope: interactive control point editing, freeform surface tools, 3dm import or export, mesh repair, rendering, assemblies, constraints solving, any GUI beyond the browser page.

Be honest in the README about what this is and is not, including that kernel failures on bad fillet radii will surface as raw OpenCascade exceptions, and show them in the UI rather than swallowing them. Include a requirements.txt or pyproject, a single run command, and note that no secrets or .env are needed because nothing leaves the machine.
